name: Slovakia
summary_text: Slovakia is workable for trans visitors. There are no traveler-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues, EU free movement, and legal gender recognition has existed for over 40 years (though medicalised and historically requiring sterilisation). Police protect Pride events. The climate is the concern. In October 2022, a radicalised teenager murdered two people outside Tepláreň, a Bratislava LGBT bar — classified as Slovakia's first modern terrorist attack. The state responded seriously (terrorism charges, official condemnation), but anti-LGBT political rhetoric intensified afterwards rather than receding: parliament advanced a bill to make legal gender recognition impossible (genetic-test-only basis), and constitutional amendments declaring gender immutable have been proposed. In July 2022 teenagers beat two men perceived as gay in Bratislava. For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning institutions, but a real threat of street hostility and a political trajectory moving against trans recognition.

sources.claim_summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (May 2023) covers Slovakia's near-vote on banning legal recognition of transgender people.

Wikipedia article on the 2022 Bratislava shooting: a double murder outside the Tepláreň LGBT bar (12 October 2022), killing Juraj Vankulič and Matúš Horváth; the perpetrator's manifesto was anti-LGBT; classified as a homophobic hate crime/terrorism; domestic and international reactions.

sources.title: In Shadow of Attack, Situation of Slovakia’s Trans Community Remains Precarious | Balkan Insight
sources.claim_summary: BIRN/Balkan Insight (Feb 2023): in the shadow of the attack, the situation of Slovakia's trans community remains precarious - long subjected to harmful practices including forced sterilisation (required for document changes), trans people remain a political target even after the terrorist attack on the LGBT bar.

sources.title: Slovak parliament should reject bill making legal gender recognition impossible
sources.claim_summary: Amnesty International (May 2023): the Slovak parliament should reject a bill making legal gender recognition impossible - trans people have been able to access LGR in Slovakia for more than 40 years, and the bill would remove this right in breach of international human-rights obligations.

Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Dunja Mijatović's letter (April 2023) to the Slovak National Council: six months after the Tepláreň attack, no discernible progress; human rights of LGBTI people appear more, not less, at risk; concerned about regressive legislative proposals including the LGR ban bill.

Slovak Spectator (May 2018): 'The biggest survey showed the lives of LGBT people' - they 'often suffer from feelings of inferiority and depression because they are rejected by the public'; only half are willing to hold their partner's hand in public; a third consider themselves Catholic.

Slovak Spectator (June 2018): same-sex married couples have the right to stay in Slovakia - the Interior Ministry responded to the CJEU judgment that a family member of an EU citizen can reside with their spouse, including same-sex spouses married elsewhere.

sources.title: Eastern and Western Europeans Differ on Importance of Religion, Views of Minorities, and Key Social Issues | Pew Research Center
sources.claim_summary: Pew Research Center (Oct 2018): 'Eastern and Western Europeans Differ on Importance of Religion, Views of Minorities, and Key Social Issues' - fewer Central and Eastern Europeans (including Slovaks) would extend marriage to gay or lesbian couples - comparative attitude data.
